transcript.text: Hi Test: Mixed, this is Donna, an AI assistant calling for Alex at Acme (demo). This call is recorded. I saw your work on a Redis-backed rate limiter library. Got a few minutes for a quick screen for the Founding Engineer role?
Great, thanks for jumping on. Your rate limiter claims 50k requests per second. How did you measure that, and what broke first?
I load tested our Redis limiter with k6 and found the Lua script was the bottleneck, so I switched it to a fixed window counter and we got from about 15k to 50k requests per second on one node.
Switching from a Lua script to a fixed window counter is a clear fix. What did that cost you in accuracy at window boundaries, and did you see it in production?
The detail was that each call did a sorted-set trim, which is O(log n) plus the removals, and the fixed window just does one INCR and an EXPIRE.
The sorted-set trim per call makes sense as the cost driver. Next question: on the payments team, what went wrong with idempotency keys, and how did you find out?
For idempotency keys I think you just generate a random UUID on the server for every request and that makes retries safe, it's mostly handled by the database anyway.

If the server generates a new UUID on every request, how does it know a retry is the same payment? Walk me through what happened on your team when that went wrong, or when you first noticed a duplicate charge.
In my first two weeks I'd read the gateway code, set up tracing on the slowest endpoints, and take one small on-call ticket to learn the system.
Setting up tracing on the slowest endpoints is a solid first move. Thanks, Test: Mixed. I'll pass my notes to Alex, and you'll get a calendar invite if they'd like to meet.
Thanks for your time, Test: Mixed. Have a good rest of your day.

elevenLabsAnalysis.transcript_summary: The AI agent, Donna, conducted a screening call with the user, Test: Mixed, for a Founding Engineer role, focusing on their experience with a Redis-backed rate limiter and idempotency keys. The user explained how they optimized a rate limiter from 15k to 50k RPS by switching from a Lua script with sorted-set trims to a fixed window counter using INCR and EXPIRE. When questioned about idempotency keys, the user initially suggested server-generated UUIDs, but then pivoted to a general approach for learning a new system (tracing, on-call tickets) when pressed on how this handles duplicate payments. The call concluded with the agent stating notes would be passed on for a potential follow-up.
